title: The RBI: one decision dressed up as three
hook:
Picture the Governor's office on Mint Street on a bad week. Oil is climbing, the rupee is sliding, foreign funds are selling Indian shares by the truckload, and somewhere in Delhi a finance ministry official is asking, politely, whether rates really need to go up before the festive season.

Most of us read the RBI through one number: the repo rate. Up is bad for stocks, down is good, done. But that is like judging a cricket captain only by the toss. The RBI is really pulling three levers at the same time: the price of money, the quantity of money, and the price of the rupee itself. In calm years they move separately and nobody notices. In a crisis, like the one we are in now, they collapse into a single decision, and the repo rate is often the least interesting part of it.

So let's open the hood.
short: The RBI controls the price of money (the repo rate), the amount of money in the system (liquidity) and leans on the price of the rupee. In a currency defence all three point the same way.
A rate hike reaches your home loan within a quarter, a company's loan much later, and your fixed deposit last. That timing decides which banks win and which lenders bleed.
Liquidity can tighten without any rate move at all: when the RBI sells dollars, rupees leave the system. Watch the overnight rate, not just the headline.
October's move was the first hike after a year of cuts, paired with tighter liquidity and currency rules. First moves in a new direction usually mean a cycle, not a one-off.

sections.heading: Lever one: the price of money
sections.html:
Start with the famous one. The repo rate is the rate at which banks can borrow overnight from the RBI by pledging government bonds. Think of it as the wholesale price of money. Banks borrow and lend among themselves around that price, and every loan in the country is priced, one way or another, off what money costs a bank for one night.

But here's the thing most people miss: the repo rate is not a single number, it's the middle of a corridor. Just below it sits the rate the RBI pays banks that park spare cash with it overnight. Just above it sits the rate at which a desperate bank can borrow in an emergency. The actual overnight rate in the market, the one traders watch, floats inside that corridor depending on how much spare cash is sloshing around. When there is too much cash, it sinks to the floor. When cash is scarce, it presses against the ceiling.

That is why a careful reader of the RBI watches the overnight rate as closely as the repo. The RBI can leave the repo untouched and still make money more expensive simply by letting the market rate drift from the floor to the ceiling. It has done exactly that, quietly, more than once.

[[fig:1]]

The diagram above is the whole chapter in one picture. Three levers on the left, the channels they travel through in the middle, and the parts of the stock market that feel them on the right. Notice how many lines cross. Every lever touches more than one channel, which is why a single RBI meeting can hit banks, carmakers, real estate developers and IT exporters in the same afternoon.

sections.heading: How a hike actually reaches you
sections.html:
When the RBI raises rates, the news anchors say borrowing gets costlier. True, but it does not happen to everyone at once, and the order matters enormously for investors.

Since 2019, banks have had to link floating-rate loans to retail borrowers and small businesses to an external benchmark, which in practice almost always means the repo rate. So when the repo goes up, your home loan rate goes up with it, typically at the next reset, within a quarter. Fast.

Big companies are a different story. Much corporate lending is still priced off each bank's internal benchmark, which reflects what the bank itself pays for funds. Those benchmarks move slowly and grudgingly, because banks compete hard for blue-chip borrowers.

And your fixed deposit? That is last in line. Banks raise deposit rates only when they have to, when they are short of deposits or a rival starts poaching customers.

A hike raises what a bank earns before it raises what the bank pays. For a while, that gap is pure profit.

That timing gap is the single most useful thing to understand about rate cycles in Indian banking. A bank with lots of externally linked retail loans and lots of cheap savings and current account deposits sees its margins widen in the first months of a hiking cycle. A lender that funds itself by borrowing from the bond market or from other banks, which is how most non-bank finance companies and housing financiers work, sees its costs rise first and its loan rates catch up later. Same hike, opposite effect.

The reverse is just as true. In a cutting cycle, like the one India had through 2025, banks with externally linked books see loan yields fall almost immediately while their deposit costs stay sticky. That margin squeeze is why bank stocks often lag in the early months of rate cuts, which surprises people who assume cuts are always good for banks.

sections.heading: Lever two: the quantity of money
sections.html:
Now the lever that gets less press but often does more work. Liquidity is simply how much spare rupee cash the banking system has after meeting its obligations. The RBI moves it in a few ways.

  • The cash reserve ratio. Banks must keep a slice of their deposits with the RBI, earning nothing. Raise that slice and money is pulled out of the system overnight. It is a blunt tool, which is precisely why the RBI uses it when it wants to be noticed.
  • Buying and selling bonds. When the RBI buys government bonds from banks it pays with fresh rupees, adding liquidity. When it sells, it soaks rupees up.
  • Selling dollars. This is the sneaky one. When the RBI sells dollars to defend the rupee, someone pays for those dollars in rupees, and those rupees vanish from the banking system. A currency defence tightens liquidity automatically, whether or not anyone announces a policy change.
  • The government's own bank balance. Tax deadlines pull cash out of banks into the government's account at the RBI; government spending puts it back. Around big tax dates, overnight rates can jump for reasons that have nothing to do with policy.

To counter that dollar-selling drain, the RBI can do something called sterilisation: buy bonds to put the rupees back. When it chooses not to, that is a message. It means the RBI is happy for money to stay tight. In October it did the opposite of sterilising: it raised the cash reserve ratio on top of selling dollars, tightening from two directions at once.

sections.heading: Lever three: the price of the rupee
sections.html:
Officially the rupee floats and the RBI only steps in to curb volatility. In practice the RBI is one of the biggest players in the currency market and it has a style. It does not try to fix a level. It tries to control the speed. A rupee that weakens gently is tolerated, even welcomed, because it helps exporters and makes imports dearer. A rupee that falls off a cliff is fought, because a disorderly fall feeds inflation, scares foreign investors and can turn into a stampede.

The RBI fights in the spot market, by selling dollars today, and in the forward market, by promising to sell dollars in the future. The forward book is worth watching because it is where the RBI hides some of its firepower: it can defend the rupee now without spending reserves now.

There is a deeper reason all three levers end up tied together. Economists call it the impossible trinity: a country cannot have free capital flows, a fixed exchange rate and an independent interest rate all at once. India allows a lot of capital to move freely. So if the RBI wants to hold the rupee steady against a surge of outflows, it eventually has to make rupees more expensive to hold, which means tighter liquidity and higher rates. That is the trap the RBI walked into this autumn, and it chose to tighten rather than let the rupee go.

One more subtlety. From late 2024 the RBI became noticeably more relaxed about letting the rupee weaken. Part of the reason was that, after years of being propped up, the rupee had become expensive against India's trading partners once you adjusted for inflation, which quietly hurts exporters. Letting it slide was a policy choice, not a loss of control. That context matters when you read today's defence: the RBI is not defending a line in the sand, it is fighting the pace.

[[fig:2]]

The chart shows the money-market rate from our own feed. You can see the long, fast climb of the 2022 hiking cycle, the plateau, and the cuts of 2025. The series stops before the October hike because the source publishes with a lag, which is exactly why the page flags it as stale rather than pretending to know the present.

sections.heading: Reading the RBI like a professional
sections.html:
Since 2016 rates have been set by a six-member Monetary Policy Committee, three from the RBI and three outside experts, with a legal mandate to keep inflation near a target band. Three things in each policy statement matter more than the decision itself.

  • The vote split. A unanimous hike is a different animal from a narrow one. Dissenters often tell you where the committee will be in two meetings.
  • The stance. One phrase, such as neutral or withdrawal of accommodation, tells the market the direction of travel. A change in stance has moved bond markets more than many rate changes.
  • The liquidity paragraph. If the statement talks about keeping liquidity in deficit, or ending a surplus, money is getting tighter regardless of the repo.

And then there is the inflation projection. If the RBI's own forecast for inflation next year is above its target, it is telling you it is not done.

sections.heading: Where it hits the stock market
sections.html:
Put it together and an RBI tightening ripples through the market in a fairly predictable order. First, bond yields rise, which makes every future rupee of profit worth less today. That hits expensive, long-duration growth stocks hardest, the companies whose value lies mostly in profits many years out. Second, rate-sensitive demand slows: home buying, car loans, consumer durables bought on instalments. Third, the banking sector splits into winners with cheap deposits and losers with expensive funding. Fourth, if the tightening succeeds in steadying the rupee, it caps the windfall exporters were enjoying from a weak currency.

None of this is instant and none of it is guaranteed. Markets move on what they expected versus what happened. A hike the market saw coming can rally stocks if the statement sounds less aggressive than feared. That is why the professionals obsess over wording.

history.title: The night the gold flew out
history.story:
In the summer of 1991 India was weeks away from defaulting on its foreign debt. Oil prices had spiked with the Gulf War, money sent home by Indians in the Gulf had dried up, and the country's foreign currency could pay for barely a few weeks of imports. To raise an emergency loan, the RBI pledged part of the nation's gold with the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan, and the gold was physically flown out of the country. When the news leaked, it was treated as a national humiliation.

That same July the RBI devalued the rupee in two sharp steps, and the new finance minister, Manmohan Singh, began dismantling the licence raj. The humiliation became the founding myth of the reform era.
history.lesson: Foreign currency reserves are not a vanity number. They are what stands between a bad year and a crisis, and the RBI has hoarded them ever since.

history.title: Rajan's first day
history.story:
In May 2013 the head of the US Federal Reserve, Ben Bernanke, merely hinted that the Fed might slow its bond buying. Money rushed out of emerging markets and the rupee went into free fall through the summer, hitting record lows almost daily. The outgoing RBI governor, D. Subbarao, had already squeezed liquidity hard to stop the bleeding, to the dismay of the government.

Then, on his very first day in office that September, Raghuram Rajan walked into the press room and announced a scheme that let banks raise dollar deposits from Indians abroad with the RBI absorbing much of the currency risk. Tens of billions of dollars poured in within weeks. The rupee turned. India was nonetheless lumped into the Fragile Five, the economies the market thought most likely to crack.
history.lesson: A clever administrative fix can buy time that rate hikes alone cannot, but the market's memory of fragility lasts for years.

history.title: The committee takes the wheel
history.story: For decades the governor set rates more or less alone, with the finance ministry breathing down his neck. In 2016 that changed: India adopted a formal inflation target and handed rate decisions to a Monetary Policy Committee with outside members. Two months after Urjit Patel became governor, the government announced demonetisation one November evening, and the RBI found itself managing a cash crunch it had not designed.
history.lesson: Since 2016, read the committee, not just the governor. The votes and the minutes are where the next move shows up first.

history.title: Wrath of the markets
history.story: In late 2018 the quarrel between the RBI and the government spilled into public view. The government wanted easier lending rules, help for small businesses and a share of the RBI's large reserves. Deputy Governor Viral Acharya gave a speech warning that governments which do not respect central bank independence will sooner or later incur the wrath of financial markets. Weeks later, Patel resigned. Shaktikanta Das, a career civil servant, took over and the temperature dropped.
history.lesson: Central bank independence is a market variable. When it is in doubt, the rupee and bond yields price the doubt.

history.title: The surprise at two in the afternoon
history.story: In May 2022, with inflation running hot after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Das called an unscheduled press conference and announced a rate hike between policy meetings, along with a higher cash reserve ratio. Nobody had seen it coming. Stocks fell sharply that afternoon. A run of large hikes followed through the year.
history.lesson: When food and fuel prices spike together, the RBI moves faster than its calendar. The schedule is a convenience, not a promise.

history.title: Cuts, then a sharp turn
history.story: Sanjay Malhotra took over at the end of 2024 and, with inflation falling, cut rates repeatedly through 2025 and flooded the system with cash. The RBI also stopped fighting every wobble in the rupee. Then came the Iran war, oil prices surged, foreign money fled and the rupee came under pressure. In October 2026 the RBI raised rates for the first time in years, raised the cash reserve ratio, opened a dollar window for oil companies and tightened rules on currency hedging.
history.lesson: The first move in a new direction is the signal. Cycles rarely end after one step.

today:
The RBI's stance as we last set it: [[val:rbi]]. Inflation is at [[val:cpi]], up [[val:cpi_3m]] in three months, driven by fuel and food. The rupee is at [[val:usdinr]] per dollar, close to its weakest ever reading of [[val:usdinr_record]], and its move over the last three months is just [[val:usdinr_3m]]: the RBI is holding it, which is exactly why money is tight.

The open question is whether October was insurance, one move to show resolve, or the start of a cycle. The answer will show up in three places before it shows up in the repo rate: the vote split at the next meeting, whether the statement talks about keeping liquidity tight, and how fast the RBI's forward dollar book grows.
sowhat:
In a tightening driven by a currency defence, the order of pain is fairly reliable.

  • Prefer banks with a big base of cheap savings and current account deposits and a book of externally linked retail loans. Their loan yields reset first.
  • Be careful with lenders that fund themselves in the bond market: non-bank finance companies, housing financiers, microlenders. Their costs rise first and their growth slows as money gets scarce.
  • Rate-sensitive demand such as housing, autos and durables tends to slow a few months after the first hikes. Developers with heavy borrowing feel it most.
  • Long-duration growth stocks on rich valuations are the most exposed to higher bond yields.
  • Exporters lose some of the cushion from a weak rupee if the defence succeeds.

The trade reverses when the RBI's language softens, liquidity is allowed back into surplus and the vote split narrows. That turn usually comes before the first cut, and the market moves on it first.
